newsitem.title: USA: FBI official pleads guilty in Ruby Ridge case.
newsitem.headline: FBI official pleads guilty in Ruby Ridge case.

text.p: A suspended FBI senior official pleaded guilty on Wednesday to obstructing justice by concealing and destroying an internal review of the deadly 1992 shootout in Ruby Ridge, Idaho.

E. Michael Kahoe, the former chief of the FBI's violent crimes section, admitted keeping from U.S. prosecutors the review they needed to prepare for the murder trial of white separatist Randy Weaver -- the key figure in the Ruby Ridge affair.
Weaver's wife and young son were shot to death by federal agents; Weaver was acquitted in the killing of a U.S. marshal.

U.S. District Judge Ricardo Urbina accepted the guilty plea and informed Kahoe, who plans to resign from the FBI in January, that he faces a maximum of 10 years in prison. No date was set for sentencing.
Prosecutor Eric Sitarchuk told the judge that Kahoe has agreed to cooperate with the long-running criminal investigation into whether FBI officials had engaged in wrongdoing or a possible cover-up.
Sitarchuk said Kahoe destroyed the review because the "FBI had problems with the Weaver case" and did not want prosecutors or defence attorneys to know it.

Weaver and his friend, Kevin Harris, were charged with the murder of Deputy U.S. Marshal William Degan, who was shot and killed in a confrontation on August 21, 1992. Weaver's son was killed in the firefight.

After the shootout, the FBI's hostage rescue team went to Ruby Ridge, and an FBI sniper fired two shots at the cabin, wounding Weaver and killing his wife. The standoff ended nine days later when Weaver surrendered.

Sitarchuk said Kahoe, who was in charge of the review, resisted, along with certain unnamed superiors, the request by prosecutors for all FBI documents. The Justice Department then ordered the FBI to turn over the documents.

The judge released Kahoe without bail until sentencing. His attorney told reporters Kahoe would have no comment as the FBI official went for the standard criminal booking procedure involving fingerprinting and photographs.
Kahoe and four other FBI officials still are suspended while the investigation, which began in August 1995, continues. One FBI agent has been cleared.
